'''Christopher McLaughlin Danforth''' is an American [[computer scientist]] and professor of [[applied mathematics]] at the [[University of Vermont]]. He is known for his work in [[computational social science]], particularly for developing the [[Hedonometer]], a tool for measuring collective mood and happiness using [[sentiment analysis]] of social media data.<ref name="bates">{{cite web|url=https://www.bates.edu/news/2020/05/01/can-peoples-tweets-help-find-coronavirus-outbreaks/|title=Can people's tweets help find coronavirus outbreaks?|publisher=Bates College News|date=May 1, 2020|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

Danforth co-directs the Computational Story Lab at the [[Vermont Complex Systems Institute]] with [[Peter Sheridan Dodds]], where he leads research on large-scale sociotechnical systems, exploring human behavior through analysis of social media and other digital data sources.<ref name="uvm_profile">{{cite web|url=https://www.uvm.edu/cems/mathstat/profile/chris-danforth|title=Chris Danforth|publisher=University of Vermont|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Danforth earned his Ph.D. in [[applied mathematics]], with early research focused on [[numerical weather prediction]] and applications of [[chaos theory]] to improve weather forecasts.<ref name="nida">{{cite web|url=https://www.ctnnortheastnode.org/members/christopher-danforth/|title=Christopher Danforth|publisher=National Drug Abuse Treatment Clinical Trials Network|date=February 2, 2021|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref> He holds the position of Professor in the Department of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Vermont and serves as Associate Director of the Vermont Complex Systems Institute.<ref name="nida" />

Danforth is also affiliated with the Vermont Advanced Computing Center, where he leads computational infrastructure development for research in [[artificial intelligence]] and [[Complex system|complex systems]].<ref name="nsf_2025">{{cite web|url=https://www.uvm.edu/uvmnews/news/uvm-attracts-55m-nsf-ai-supercomputer-underground-robots-health-science|title=UVM Attracts $5.5M from NSF for AI Supercomputer, Underground Robots, Health Science|publisher=University of Vermont News|date=July 15, 2025|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

== Research ==

=== Hedonometer and sentiment analysis ===
In 2007, Danforth collaborated with Peter Sheridan Dodds to develop the Hedonometer, an instrument designed to measure happiness and emotional states in large populations through analysis of social media text.<ref name="burlington">{{cite web|url=https://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/life/2020/10/29/uvm-happiness-calculator-research-highlighted-reply-all-podcast/6069635002/|title=UVM 'happiness calculator' research highlighted in popular Reply All podcast|author=Ethan Bakuli|publisher=The Burlington Free Press|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref> The project involved surveying native speakers of multiple languages to rate words on a happiness scale, creating a weighted dictionary of emotional valence for approximately 10,000 words in ten languages.<ref name="datainnovation">{{cite web|url=https://datainnovation.org/2015/03/5-qs-for-chris-danforth-co-founder-of-the-computational-story-lab/|title=5 Q's for Chris Danforth, Co-Director of the Computational Story Lab|publisher=Center for Data Innovation|date=March 20, 2015|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

The Hedonometer measures real-time emotional trends by analyzing text from [[Twitter]] and other social media platforms. Research using the tool has examined emotional responses to major events, geographical variations in happiness, and temporal patterns in collective mood.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Peter Sheridan Dodds|author2=Kameron Decker Harris|author3=Isabel M. Kloumann|author4=Catherine A. Bliss|author5=Christopher M. Danforth|title=Temporal Patterns of Happiness and Information in a Global Social Network: Hedonometrics and Twitter|journal=PLOS ONE|year=2011|volume=6|issue=12|article-number=e26752|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0026752|doi-access=free |pmid=22163266|pmc=3232192 |arxiv=1101.5120 |bibcode=2011PLoSO...626752D }}</ref> Studies have documented applications in analyzing events such as the Ferguson protests, where the tool identified significant shifts in word usage patterns reflecting community sentiment.<ref name="datainnovation" />

=== Mental health detection ===
Danforth's research has explored the use of social media data for early detection of mental health conditions. In collaboration with psychologist Andrew Reece of [[Harvard University]], he conducted a 2017 study analyzing Instagram photographs to identify markers of [[Depression (mood)|depression]]. The research examined 43,950 photos from 166 participants and used [[machine learning]] to analyze features including color composition, brightness, filter usage, and face detection.<ref name="instagram">{{cite journal|author1=Andrew G. Reece|author2=Christopher M. Danforth|title=Instagram photos reveal predictive markers of depression|journal=EPJ Data Science|year=2017|volume=6|issue=1|page=15|doi=10.1140/epjds/s13688-017-0110-z|doi-access=free|hdl=20.500.14849/591|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

The study found that photographs posted by individuals with depression tended to be bluer, darker, and grayer in color compared to those posted by non-depressed individuals. The computational model achieved a 70% accuracy rate in identifying depression, outperforming the average 42% diagnostic success rate of general practitioners in unassisted depression diagnosis.<ref name="sciencedaily">{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/08/170809083209.htm|title=When you're blue, so are your Instagram photos|publisher=ScienceDaily|date=August 9, 2017|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref> Notably, the model could detect signs of depression in photographs posted before individuals received clinical diagnoses, suggesting potential for early screening applications.<ref name="instagram" />

=== Other research contributions ===
Danforth's work spans multiple areas of computational science and complex systems. He has published research on:

* Applications of [[chaos theory]] to numerical weather prediction and climate modeling.<ref name="uvm_profile" />
* Analysis of information spreading and [[social contagion]] in online networks
* Computational approaches to understanding narrative structure and storytelling.
* The "[[Wikipedia philosophy phenomenon]]", where following the first link in Wikipedia articles often leads to the Philosophy article.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://psmag.com/news/all-wikipedia-roads-lead-to-philosophy-but-some-of-them-go-through-southeast-europe-first/|title=All Wikipedia Roads Lead to Philosophy, but Some of Them Go Through Southeast Europe First|author=Nathan Collins|publisher=Pacific Standard|date=May 9, 2016|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

== Computational Story Lab ==
Danforth co-directs the Computational Story Lab with Peter Sheridan Dodds, a research group focused on large-scale, system-level problems across sociology, nonlinear dynamics, networks, ecology, and physics. The lab's research combines observational data, mathematical models, and computational simulations to understand complex phenomena.<ref name="compstorylab">{{cite web|url=https://compstorylab.org/about/|title=About|publisher=Computational Story Lab|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

The lab has developed several tools and datasets for the research community, including:
* '''Hedonometer''': A public website providing real-time happiness measurements from Twitter data<ref>{{cite web|url=https://hedonometer.org/about.html|title=About the Hedonometer|publisher=Hedonometer.org|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>
* '''StoryWrangler''': A platform for analyzing phrase popularity across 150 billion tweets

== Funding and support ==
Danforth's research has been supported by multiple organizations, including the [[National Science Foundation]], the [[National Institutes of Health]], the [[James S. McDonnell Foundation]], the [[Office of Naval Research]], [[NASA]], and [[MITRE Corporation]].<ref name="dodds_research">{{cite web|url=https://www.uvm.edu/pdodds/research/|title=Research|author=Peter Sheridan Dodds|publisher=University of Vermont|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

In 2023, as part of a group of researchers in the Vermont Complex Systems Institute, he helped procure a [[National Science Foundation]] award to study the science of stories. This 5-year grant was called The Science of Online Corpora, Knowledge, and Stories (SOCKS).<ref>{{Cite web |title=UVM Earns $20M Research Grant to ‘Harness the Data Revolution’ |url=https://www.uvm.edu/uvmnews/news/uvm-earns-20m-research-grant-harness-data-revolution |access-date=2026-04-16 |website=www.uvm.edu |language=en}}</ref>

In 2025, Danforth led a team that received a $2.1 million grant from the National Science Foundation to create IceCore, a high-performance computing cluster for artificial intelligence research. The system is designed to support approximately 1,000 researchers across Vermont and New England studying topics including infectious diseases, computational social science, and large language models.<ref name="nsf_2025" />

== Teaching ==
At the University of Vermont, Danforth teaches courses in applied mathematics, including linear algebra, numerical analysis, nonlinear dynamics, ordinary differential equations, and data ethics.<ref name="danforth_homepage">{{cite web|url=http://www.uvm.edu/~cdanfort/|title=Chris Danforth|publisher=University of Vermont|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref> He has developed video lecture series on nonlinear dynamics that are freely available online.<ref name="danforth_homepage" />

== Publications ==
According to [[Google Scholar]], Danforth's work has been cited over 10,700 times.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=huQnquIAAAAJ&hl=en|title=Chris Danforth - Google Scholar|publisher=Google Scholar|access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref> His most highly cited works include research on temporal patterns of happiness in social networks, the universal positivity bias in human language, and computational methods for mental health screening.
